verses.zh: 雅各住在迦南地，就是他父亲寄居的地。
verses.en: But Jacob lived in the land where his father had stayed,[NOTE:1] in the land of Canaan.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “the land of the sojournings of his father.”

The next section begins with the heading This is the account of Jacob in Gen 37:2, so this verse actually forms part of the preceding section as a concluding contrast with Esau and his people. In contrast to all the settled and expanded population of Esau, Jacob was still moving about in the land without a permanent residence and without kings. Even if the Edomite king list was added later (as the reference to kings in Israel suggests), its placement here in contrast to Jacob and his descendants is important. Certainly the text deals with Esau before dealing with Jacob—that is the pattern. But the detail is so great in chap. 36 that the contrast cannot be missed.

verses.zh: 雅各的记略如下。约瑟十七岁与他哥哥们一同牧羊。他是个童子，与他父亲的妾辟拉、悉帕的儿子们常在一处。约瑟将他哥哥们的恶行报给他们的父亲。
verses.en: This is the account of Jacob.Joseph, his seventeen-year-old son,[NOTE:1] was taking care of[NOTE:2] the flocks with his brothers. Now he was a youngster[NOTE:3] working with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives.[NOTE:4] Joseph brought back a bad report about them[NOTE:5] to their father.
notes: Heb “a son of seventeen years.” The word “son” is in apposition to the name “Joseph.”
Or “tending”; Heb “shepherding” or “feeding.”
Or perhaps “a helper.” The significance of this statement is unclear. It may mean “now the lad was with,” or it may suggest Joseph was like a servant to them.
Heb “and he [was] a young man with the sons of Bilhah and with the sons of Zilpah, the wives of his father.”

Heb “their bad report.” The pronoun is an objective genitive, specifying that the bad or damaging report was about the brothers.sn Some interpreters portray Joseph as a tattletale for bringing back a bad report about them [i.e., his brothers], but the entire Joseph story has some of the characteristics of wisdom literature. Joseph is presented in a good light—not because he was perfect, but because the narrative is showing how wisdom rules. In light of that, this section portrays Joseph as faithful to his father in little things, even though unpopular—and so he will eventually be given authority over greater things.

verses.zh: 以色列原来爱约瑟过于爱他的众子，因为约瑟是他年老生的；他给约瑟做了一件彩衣。
verses.en: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons[NOTE:1] because he was a son born to him late in life,[NOTE:2] and he made a special[NOTE:3] tunic for him.
notes: The statement Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons brings forward a motif that played an important role in the family of Isaac—parental favoritism. Jacob surely knew what that had done to him and his brother Esau, and to his own family. But now he showers affection on Rachel’s son Joseph.tn The disjunctive clause provides supplemental information vital to the story. It explains in part the brothers’ animosity toward Joseph.
Heb “a son of old age was he to him.” This expression means “a son born to him when he [i.e., Jacob] was old.”

It is not clear what this tunic was like because the meaning of the Hebrew word that describes it is uncertain. The idea that it was a coat of many colors comes from the Greek translation of the OT. An examination of cognate terms in Semitic suggests it was either a coat or tunic with long sleeves (cf. NEB, NRSV), or a tunic that was richly embroidered (cf. NIV). It set Joseph apart as the favored one.

verses.zh: 约瑟的哥哥们见父亲爱约瑟过于爱他们，就恨约瑟，不与他说和睦的话。
verses.en: When Joseph’s[NOTE:1] brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them,[NOTE:2] they hated Joseph[NOTE:3] and were not able to speak to him kindly.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “his”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “of his brothers.” This is redundant in contemporary English and has been replaced in the translation by the pronoun “them.”
Heb “him”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “speak to him for peace.”

verses.zh: 约瑟做了一梦，告诉他哥哥们，他们就越发恨他。
verses.en: Joseph[NOTE:1] had a dream,[NOTE:2] and when he told his brothers about it[NOTE:3] they hated him even more.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “and he”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “dreamed a dream.”

Some interpreters see Joseph as gloating over his brothers, but the text simply says he told his brothers about it (i.e., the dream). The text gives no warrant for interpreting his manner as arrogant or condescending. It seems normal that he would share a dream with the family.
The construction uses a hendiadys, “they added to hate,” meaning they hated him even more.

verses.zh: 约瑟对他们说：「请听我所做的梦：
verses.en: He said to them, “Listen to this dream I had:[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “hear this dream which I dreamed.”

verses.zh: 我们在田里捆禾稼，我的捆起来站着，你们的捆来围着我的捆下拜。」
verses.en: There we were,[NOTE:1] binding sheaves of grain in the middle of the field. Suddenly my sheaf rose up and stood upright and your sheaves surrounded my sheaf and bowed down[NOTE:2] to it!”
notes: All three clauses in this dream report begin with וְהִנֵּה (vehinneh, “and look”), which lends vividness to the report. This is represented in the translation by the expression “there we were.”
The verb means “to bow down to the ground.” It is used to describe worship and obeisance to masters.

verses.zh: 他的哥哥们回答说：「难道你真要作我们的王吗？难道你真要管辖我们吗？」他们就因为他的梦和他的话越发恨他。
verses.en: Then his brothers asked him, “Do you really think you will rule over us or have dominion over us?”[NOTE:1] They hated him even more[NOTE:2] because of his dream and because of what he said.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Ruling, will you rule over us, or reigning, will you reign over us?” The statement has a poetic style, with the two questions being in synonymous parallelism. Both verbs in this statement are preceded by the infinitive absolute, which lends emphasis. It is as if Joseph’s brothers said, “You don’t really think you will rule over us, do you? You don’t really think you will have dominion over us, do you?”
This construction is identical to the one in Gen 37:5.

The response of Joseph’s brothers is understandable, given what has already been going on in the family. But here there is a hint of uneasiness—they hated him because of his dream and because of his words. The dream bothered them, as well as his telling them. And their words in the rhetorical question are ironic, for this is exactly what would happen. The dream was God’s way of revealing it.

verses.zh: 后来他又做了一梦，也告诉他的哥哥们说：「看哪，我又做了一梦，梦见太阳、月亮，与十一个星向我下拜。」
verses.en: Then he had another dream,[NOTE:1] and told it to his brothers. “Look,”[NOTE:2] he said. “I had another dream. The sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”
notes: Heb “And he dreamed yet another dream.”

Heb “and he said, ‘Look.’” The order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons. Both clauses of the dream report begin with הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”), which lends vividness to the report.

verses.zh: 约瑟将这梦告诉他父亲和他哥哥们，他父亲就责备他说：「你做的这是甚么梦！难道我和你母亲、你弟兄果然要来俯伏在地，向你下拜吗？」
verses.en: When he told his father and his brothers, his father rebuked him, saying, “What is this dream that you had?[NOTE:1] Will I, your mother, and your brothers really come and bow down to you?”[NOTE:2]
notes: The question What is this dream that you had? expresses Jacob’s dismay at what he perceives to be Joseph’s audacity.

Heb “Coming, will we come, I and your mother and your brothers, to bow down to you to the ground?” The verb “come” is preceded by the infinitive absolute, which lends emphasis. It is as if Jacob said, “You don’t really think we will come…to bow down…do you?”

verses.zh: 他哥哥们都嫉妒他，他父亲却把这话存在心里。
verses.en: His brothers were jealous[NOTE:1] of him, but his father kept in mind what Joseph said.[NOTE:2]
notes: Joseph’s brothers were already jealous of him, but this made it even worse. Such jealousy easily leads to action, as the next episode in the story shows. Yet dreams were considered a form of revelation, and their jealousy was not only of the favoritism of their father, but of the dreams. This is why Jacob kept the matter in mind.
Heb “kept the word.” The referent of the Hebrew term “word” has been specified as “what Joseph said” in the translation for clarity, and the words “in mind” have been supplied for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 约瑟的哥哥们往示剑去放他们父亲的羊。
verses.en: When his brothers had gone to graze their father’s flocks near Shechem,

verses.zh: 以色列对约瑟说：「你哥哥们不是在示剑放羊吗？你来，我要打发你往他们那里去。」约瑟说：「我在这里。」
verses.en: Israel said to Joseph, “Your brothers[NOTE:1] are grazing the flocks near Shechem. Come, I will send you to them.” “I’m ready,”[NOTE:2] Joseph replied.[NOTE:3]
notes: The text uses an interrogative clause: “Are not your brothers,” which means “your brothers are.”
With these words Joseph is depicted here as an obedient son who is ready to do what his father commands.

Heb “and he said, ‘Here I am.’” The referent of the pronoun “he” (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity, and the order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 以色列说：「你去看看你哥哥们平安不平安，群羊平安不平安，就回来报信给我。」于是打发他出希伯仑谷，他就往示剑去了。
verses.en: So Jacob[NOTE:1] said to him, “Go now and check on[NOTE:2] the welfare[NOTE:3] of your brothers and of the flocks, and bring me word.” So Jacob[NOTE:4] sent him from the valley of Hebron.
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “see.”
Heb “peace.”
Heb “he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 有人遇见他在田野走迷了路，就问他说：「你找甚么？」
verses.en: When Joseph reached Shechem,[NOTE:1] a man found him wandering[NOTE:2] in the field, so the man asked him, “What are you looking for?”
notes: Heb “and he [i.e., Joseph] went to Shechem.” The referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity. In Hebrew, these are the last two words of verse 14, but they have been carried over to verse 15 in the NET for stylistic reasons.
Heb “and a man found him and look, he was wandering in the field.” By the use of וְהִנֵּה (vehinneh, “and look”), the narrator invites the reader to see the action through this unnamed man’s eyes.

verses.zh: 他说：「我找我的哥哥们，求你告诉我，他们在何处放羊。」
verses.en: He replied, “I’m looking for my brothers. Please tell[NOTE:1] me where they are grazing their flocks.”
notes: The imperative in this sentence has more of the nuance of a request than a command.

verses.zh: 那人说：「他们已经走了，我听见他们说要往多坍去。」约瑟就去追赶他哥哥们，遇见他们在多坍。
verses.en: The man said, “They left this area,[NOTE:1] for I heard them say, ‘Let’s go to Dothan.’” So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
notes: Heb “they traveled from this place.”

verses.zh: 他们远远地看见他，趁他还没有走到跟前，大家就同谋要害死他，
verses.en: Now Joseph’s brothers[NOTE:1] saw him from a distance, and before he reached them, they plotted to kill him.
notes: Heb “and they”; the referent (Joseph’s brothers) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 彼此说：「你看！那做梦的来了。
verses.en: They said to one another, “Here comes this master of dreams![NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “Look, this master of dreams is coming.” The brothers’ words have a sarcastic note and indicate that they resent his dreams.

verses.zh: 来吧！我们将他杀了，丢在一个坑里，就说有恶兽把他吃了。我们且看他的梦将来怎么样。」
verses.en: Come now, let’s kill him, throw him into one of the cisterns, and then say that a wild[NOTE:1] animal ate him. Then we’ll see how his dreams turn out!”[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew word can sometimes carry the nuance “evil,” but when used of an animal it refers to a dangerous wild animal.
Heb “what his dreams will be.”

verses.zh: 流便听见了，要救他脱离他们的手，说：「我们不可害他的性命」；
verses.en: When Reuben heard this, he rescued Joseph[NOTE:1] from their hands,[NOTE:2] saying,[NOTE:3] “Let’s not take his life!”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “him”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
From their hands. The instigators of this plot may have been the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah (see v. 2).
Heb “and he said.”
Heb “we must not strike him down [with respect to] life.”

verses.zh: 又说：「不可流他的血，可以把他丢在这野地的坑里，不可下手害他。」流便的意思是要救他脱离他们的手，把他归还他的父亲。
verses.en: Reuben continued,[NOTE:1] “Don’t shed blood! Throw him into this cistern that is here in the wilderness, but don’t lay a hand on him.”[NOTE:2] (Reuben said this[NOTE:3] so he could rescue Joseph[NOTE:4] from them[NOTE:5] and take him back to his father.)
notes: Heb “and Reuben said to them.”
The verbs translated shed, throw, and lay sound alike in Hebrew; the repetition of similar sounds draws attention to Reuben’s words.
The words “Reuben said this” are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “him”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “from their hands” (cf. v. 21). This expression has been translated as “them” here for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 约瑟到了他哥哥们那里，他们就剥了他的外衣，就是他穿的那件彩衣，
verses.en: When Joseph reached his brothers, they stripped him[NOTE:1] of his tunic, the special tunic that he wore.
notes: Heb “Joseph”; the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“him”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 把他丢在坑里；那坑是空的，里头没有水。
verses.en: Then they took him and threw him into the cistern. (Now the cistern was empty;[NOTE:1] there was no water in it.)
notes: The disjunctive clause gives supplemental information that helps the reader or hearer to picture what happened.

verses.zh: 他们坐下吃饭，举目观看，见有一伙米甸的以实玛利人从基列来，用骆驼驮着香料、乳香、没药，要带下埃及去。
verses.en: When they sat down to eat their food, they looked up[NOTE:1] and saw[NOTE:2] a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh down to Egypt.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “lifted up their eyes.”
Heb “and they saw and look.” By the use of וְהִנֵּה (vehinneh, “and look”), the narrator invites the reader to see the event through the eyes of the brothers.
Heb “and their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh, going to go down to Egypt.”

verses.zh: 犹大对众弟兄说：「我们杀我们的兄弟，藏了他的血有甚么益处呢？
verses.en: Then Judah said to his brothers, “What profit is there if we kill our brother and cover up his blood?

verses.zh: 我们不如将他卖给以实玛利人，不可下手害他；因为他是我们的兄弟，我们的骨肉。」众弟兄就听从了他。
verses.en: Come, let’s sell him to the Ishmaelites, but let’s not lay a hand on him,[NOTE:1] for after all, he is our brother, our own flesh.” His brothers agreed.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “let not our hand be upon him.”
Heb “listened.”

verses.zh: 有些米甸的商人从那里经过，哥哥们就把约瑟从坑里拉上来，讲定二十舍客勒银子，把约瑟卖给以实玛利人。他们就把约瑟带到埃及去了。
verses.en: So when the Midianite[NOTE:1] merchants passed by, Joseph’s brothers pulled[NOTE:2] him[NOTE:3] out of the cistern and sold him to the Ishmaelites for 20 pieces of silver. The Ishmaelites[NOTE:4] then took Joseph to Egypt.
notes: On the close relationship between Ishmaelites (v. 25) and Midianites, see Judg 8:24.

Heb “they drew and they lifted up.” The referent (Joseph’s brothers) has been specified in the translation for clarity; otherwise the reader might assume the Midianites had pulled Joseph from the cistern (but cf. NAB).
Heb “Joseph” (both here and in the following clause); the proper name has been replaced both times by the pronoun “him” in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “they”; the referent (the Ishmaelites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 流便回到坑边，见约瑟不在坑里，就撕裂衣服，
verses.en: Later Reuben returned to the cistern to find that Joseph was not in it![NOTE:1] He tore his clothes,
notes: Heb “and look, Joseph was not in the cistern.” By the use of וְהִנֵּה (vehinneh, “and look”), the narrator invites the reader to see the situation through Reuben’s eyes.

verses.zh: 回到兄弟们那里，说：「童子没有了。我往哪里去才好呢？」
verses.en: returned to his brothers, and said, “The boy isn’t there! And I, where can I go?”

verses.zh: 他们宰了一只公山羊，把约瑟的那件彩衣染了血，
verses.en: So they took Joseph’s tunic, killed a young goat,[NOTE:1] and dipped the tunic in the blood.
notes: It was with two young goats that Jacob deceived his father (Gen 27:9); now with a young goat his sons continue the deception that dominates this family.

verses.zh: 打发人送到他们的父亲那里，说：「我们捡了这个；请认一认是你儿子的外衣不是？」
verses.en: Then they brought the special tunic to their father[NOTE:1] and said, “We found this. Determine now whether it is your son’s tunic or not.”
notes: Heb “and they sent the special tunic and they brought [it] to their father.” The text as it stands is problematic. It sounds as if they sent the tunic on ahead and then came and brought it to their father. Some emend the second verb to a Qal form and read “and they came.” In this case, they sent the tunic on ahead.

verses.zh: 他认得，就说：「这是我儿子的外衣。有恶兽把他吃了，约瑟被撕碎了！撕碎了！」
verses.en: He recognized it and exclaimed, “It is my son’s tunic! A wild animal has eaten him![NOTE:1] Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!”
notes: A wild animal has eaten him. Jacob draws this conclusion on his own without his sons actually having to lie with their words (see v. 20). Dipping the tunic in the goat’s blood was the only deception needed.

verses.zh: 雅各便撕裂衣服，腰间围上麻布，为他儿子悲哀了多日。
verses.en: Then Jacob tore his clothes, put on sackcloth,[NOTE:1] and mourned for his son many days.
notes: Heb “and put sackcloth on his loins.”

verses.zh: 他的儿女都起来安慰他，他却不肯受安慰，说：「我必悲哀着下阴间，到我儿子那里。」约瑟的父亲就为他哀哭。
verses.en: All his sons and daughters stood by[NOTE:1] him to console him, but he refused to be consoled. “No,” he said, “I will go to the grave mourning my son.”[NOTE:2] So Joseph’s[NOTE:3] father wept for him.
notes: Heb “arose, stood”; which here suggests that they stood by him in his time of grief.
Heb “and he said, ‘Indeed I will go down to my son mourning to Sheol.’” Sheol was viewed as the place where departed spirits went after death.
Heb “his”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 米甸人带约瑟到埃及，把他卖给法老的内臣―护卫长波提乏。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] in Egypt the Midianites[NOTE:2] sold Joseph[NOTE:3] to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh’s officials, the captain of the guard.[NOTE:4]
notes: The disjunctive clause formally signals closure for this episode of Joseph’s story, which will be resumed in Gen 39.

The MT spells the name of the merchants as מְדָנִים (medanim, “Medanites”) rather than מִדְיָנִים (midyanim, “Midianites”) as in v. 28. It is likely that the letter י (yod) was accidentally omitted in the MT. The LXX, Vulgate, Smr, and Syriac read “Midianites” here. Some prefer to read “Medanites” both here and in v. 28, but Judg 8:24, which identifies the Midianites and Ishmaelites, favors the reading “Midianites.”
Heb “him”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The expression captain of the guard might indicate that Potiphar was the chief executioner. The noun "guard" derives from a verb meaning to slaughter.
